source.title: Push the Student to Learn Right: Progressive Gradient Correcting by Meta-learner on Corrupted Labels
source.authors: Jun Shu; Qi Xie; Li-Xuan Yi; Qian Zhao; Sanping Zhou; Zong-Ben Xu; De-Yu Meng

record.file_problem: The supplied text contains the full paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study evaluates noisy-label training and reports test accuracy across corruption rates, a related measure of V4. It does not report a direct random-label fit test or training accuracy values in text.
record.gate_note: The paper reports results for multiple reweighting methods, but only BaseModel rows are included because the claim concerns standard, unmodified networks. Results cited from prior work are excluded. Training-accuracy curves appear only in figures and are not extracted as values.
record.test_reason: The BaseModel experiments directly train standard networks with SGD on randomly corrupted labels and measure test accuracy across corruption rates. They test the degradation component of V4 using the original uniform-corruption setup; perfect training fit is not established by the supplied text.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that learning an explicit sample-weighting function from clean meta-data improves robustness to class imbalance, corrupted labels, and more complicated real-world data biases.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains classifier networks with a learned sample-weighting method guided by a clean meta-data set; BaseModel is directly trained on biased training data. It does not reproduce the original random-label experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Dataset and corruption type/rate vary; model architecture differs by setting (WRN-28-10 for uniform noise, ResNet-32 for flip noise).
record.peer_reviewed: 33rd Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2019), Vancouver, Canada
record.problems: The paper does not report textual training-accuracy values for BaseModel under corruption; curves are figure-only. The highest reported corruption rates are 60% uniform and 40% flip, short of complete random labeling. Results average 5 repetitions.
record.rows_left_out: No table rows omitted. Figure 7 training/test accuracy curves are not entered as numeric rows because the values are figure-only; the text describes baseline overfitting but gives no exact curve values.

untested.parts: Completely random labels, near-zero training error, chance test performance, and unchanged hyperparameters in that condition.
Training-time comparisons between true and random labels and convergence slowing across corruption fractions. The reported method speedups compare weighting algorithms instead.
Fitting shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian inputs.

Perfect training fit at every corruption rate, degradation through 100% corruption to chance, and a sufficiently dense sweep to establish smoothness. Figure 7 is declared omitted and its numerical training accuracies cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
Controlled removal or addition of regularization and augmentation, random-label fitting under those interventions, and clean-label generalization after their removal.

Direct comparison of when clean patterns and noisy labels are learned. Appendix G reports later overfitting and test degradation, but does not separately measure clean-pattern learning and noisy-label memorization.

missing.what: Additional BaseModel WRN-28-10 test-accuracy results under flip noise on both CIFAR datasets. Figure 4 includes this architecture beyond Table 3; curve values cannot be read from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: The original limits_scope verdict mistakes untested components for demonstrated failures. Lower test accuracy under greater corruption is predicted by V4 and does not warrant a partial state. Appendix G explicitly reports baseline overfitting after learning-rate decay, but neither that statement nor the extracted figure text establishes zero training error.

versions.untested_parts: No completely random labeling condition or textual result showing training error and test error at chance.
No comparison of training time for true versus random labels, or convergence time across corruption fractions for unmodified networks.
No shuffled-pixel or Gaussian-noise input experiments.

The study varies label corruption and reports test accuracy, but does not state in text that the unmodified networks fit every noisy training set perfectly; training-accuracy curves are figure-only. It does not test corruption all the way to 100%.
No test of whether regularization or augmentation prevents random-label fitting or whether removing them harms true-label generalization.
No analysis of whether real-label patterns are learned before noisy or random labels.

rows.subject: WRN-28-10 (BaseModel)
rows.operation_detail: Trained directly on training data with uniform label noise; test classification accuracy reported.
rows.check: Correct value; this clean-label control supplies the baseline for R2–R3 but alone cannot establish degradation or perfect training fit.

rows.subject: WRN-28-10 (BaseModel)
rows.operation_detail: Trained directly on training data with uniform label noise; test classification accuracy reported.
rows.check: Test accuracy falls from 95.60% to 68.07%, as V4 predicts. This measures only the test-degradation component, not incomplete random-label fitting.

relationships.reason: Accuracy decreases monotonically: 95.60→68.07→53.12% and 79.95→51.11→30.92%, remaining above chance (R1–R6).
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy declined successively from 95.60% to 68.07% to 53.12% on CIFAR-10 and from 79.95% to 51.11% to 30.92% on CIFAR-100, remaining above chance.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: BaseModel on CIFAR-10 and CIFAR-100 at the reported uniform and flip noise rates
reader_labels.reason: Test accuracy decreases as the reported corruption rate rises, but results stop at 60% uniform and 40% flip noise and do not establish perfect training fit or behavior at 100% corruption (R1–R12).
